title: 4A. Taxonomic composition (track A: insects)
text:
Summarise taxonomic composition across habitats and months using stacked barplots.

Select samples
We keep the rows of the counts table that belong to the samples selected in step 3. semi_join() filters one table by another, and DuckDB does the work without reading the whole table into R:
selected <- duckdb_tibble(eventID = samples$eventID, .prudence = "stingy")
counts_selected <- merged$counts |> semi_join(selected, by = "eventID")


Sum reads by taxonomy
sum_clades_long() from step 2 can be limited to one taxonomic rank and to these samples. The result is small enough to bring into R. We then add the habitat and month of each sample:
get_composition <- function(rank) {
  composition <- sum_clades_long(counts_selected, merged$asvs, ranks = rank) |>
    as.data.frame()
  merge(composition, samples[c("eventID", "habitat", "month")], by = "eventID")
}
Only the available ranks work here: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species and otu.


Define the barplot function
The function below identifies the most abundant taxa across the selected samples, calculates their mean relative abundance for each habitat and month, and draws stacked barplots with ggplot2. ggplot2 draws directly from a table with one row per value: each row of monthly becomes one segment of a bar.
plot_barplots <- function(rank, top_x = 10) {
  composition <- get_composition(rank)

  # Absent taxa have no rows, so a mean is the sum divided by the number of samples
  totals <- tapply(composition$norm, composition$clade, sum)
  top <- names(sort(totals / nrow(samples), decreasing = TRUE))[1:top_x]

  monthly <- aggregate(norm ~ clade + habitat + month, composition[composition$clade %in% top, ], sum)
  n_samples <- aggregate(eventID ~ habitat + month, samples, length)
  monthly <- merge(monthly, n_samples)
  monthly$share <- monthly$norm / monthly$eventID

  # Reversed levels put the most abundant taxon at the bottom of each bar
  monthly$clade <- factor(monthly$clade, levels = rev(top))
  monthly$month <- factor(monthly$month, levels = 1:12, labels = month.abb)
  monthly$habitat <- factor(monthly$habitat, levels = names(habitat_cols))

  mycols <- colorRampPalette(c(
    "#a6cee3", "#1f78b4", "#b2df8a", "#33a02c",
    "#fb9a99", "#e31a1c", "#fdbf6f", "#ff7f00",
    "#cab2d6", "#6a3d9a", "#ffff99", "#b15928"
  ))

  ggplot(monthly, aes(x = month, y = share, fill = clade)) +
    geom_col(colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.2) +
    facet_wrap(~habitat, ncol = 2) +
    scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(mycols(top_x), top), breaks = top, name = rank) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean share of reads") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}
The same paired sample set selected in step 3 is used both to select the most abundant taxa and to calculate the habitat-by-month averages.


Example: plot top orders
Plot the eight most abundant orders across habitats and months:
plot_barplots(rank = "order", top_x = 8)
Flies (Diptera) dominate the reads in all habitats, especially in the alpine samples and early in the season. Note that these are shares of the reads, not of the number of individuals or the biomass. Empty months had no selected samples in that habitat.

title: 5A. Community differences (track A: insects)
text:
Analyse differences in community composition between samples — beta diversity — using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).
We use counts_selected, the read counts of the samples selected in step 3, from step 4.

Aggregate ASVs to clusters
In addition to ASV taxonomy and BOLD BINs, the IBA data also include project-specific cluster assignments in the associatedSequences column. Most pairs of samples share few ASVs, so comparing them at ASV level says rather little. We therefore sum the reads of each cluster in each sample, which is a join followed by a grouped sum.
The cluster assignments are read from loaded, because merge_long() keeps only the attributes that describe the ASV itself, and associatedSequences is specific to each dataset:
clusters <- loaded$asvs |> distinct(taxonID, cluster = associatedSequences)

cluster_counts <- counts_selected |>
  inner_join(clusters, by = "taxonID") |>
  summarise(quant = sum(organismQuantity, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(eventID, cluster)) |>
  transmute(sample = eventID, taxon = cluster, quant)
The new names, sample, taxon and quant, are the ones that ecolongr expects by default. Nothing has been computed yet: cluster_counts is still a query.


Calculate Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
Bray-Curtis dissimilarity compares the abundances of taxa in two samples, from 0 for identical communities to 1 for communities with nothing in common. We first turn the counts into relative abundances, so that sequencing depth does not affect the comparison, and then calculate the dissimilarities:
bray <- cluster_counts |>
  el_decostand("total") |>
  el_vegdist("bray", samples = samples$eventID)
el_decostand() and el_vegdist() work like decostand() and vegdist() in the vegan package, but on our table, without reading it into R. samples = makes the result follow the order of the rows in samples, which we rely on when plotting. The result is an ordinary dist object, with one value per pair of samples, that vegan and base R can use.


Run PCoA
Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) represents the dissimilarities among samples in a smaller number of dimensions:
pcoa <- cmdscale(bray, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

# Share of the positive eigenvalues held by each of the first two axes
axis_share <- pcoa$eig[1:2] / sum(pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0])
round(100 * axis_share, 1)
Unlike the distances, PCoA needs the full matrix of dissimilarities in memory, and its run time grows quickly with the number of samples. That is fine for the samples we use here, but for many thousands of samples you may prefer el_rda(), a PCA that runs directly on the counts table.


Prepare colour scales
habitat_cols was already created in step 3. We add continuous colour scales for sampling date and latitude, plus colours for the two extraction methods:
ramp <- colorRampPalette(rev(c(
  "#D73027", "#FC8D59", "#FEE090", "#FFFFBF", "#E0F3F8", "#91BFDB", "#4575B4"
)))

yday_range <- min(samples$yday):max(samples$yday)
color_yday <- ramp(length(yday_range))
yday_index <- samples$yday - min(yday_range) + 1

lat_range <- floor(min(samples$decimalLatitude)):ceiling(max(samples$decimalLatitude))
color_lat <- ramp(length(lat_range))
lat_index <- round(samples$decimalLatitude) - min(lat_range) + 1

method_cols <- c(
  IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "#e76f51",
  IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "#2a9d8f"
)
method_labs <- c(
  IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "homogenate",
  IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "lysate"
)
For the legends, latitude is shown at 2-degree intervals and sampling date by month:
lat_ticks <- seq(ceiling(min(lat_range) / 2) * 2, max(lat_range), by = 2)

month_ticks  <- sort(tapply(samples$yday, samples$month, min))
month_labels <- month.abb[as.integer(names(month_ticks))]


Plot PCoA results
We plot the same PCoA four times, colouring samples by sampling date, habitat, latitude and extraction method:
plot_pcoa <- function() {
  xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(100 * axis_share[1]), "%)")
  ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(100 * axis_share[2]), "%)")
  x <- pcoa$points[, 1]
  y <- pcoa$points[, 2]

  par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 6), xpd = TRUE)

  # Panel: colour by year-day
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = color_yday[yday_index], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by year-day")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = color_yday[month_ticks - min(yday_range) + 1],
         legend = month_labels)

  # Panel: colour by habitat
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = habitat_cols[samples$habitat], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by habitat")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = habitat_cols, legend = names(habitat_cols))

  # Panel: colour by latitude
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = color_lat[lat_index], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by latitude")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = color_lat[lat_ticks - min(lat_range) + 1],
         legend = lat_ticks)

  # Panel: colour by extraction method
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = method_cols[samples$method], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by extraction method")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = method_cols, legend = method_labs)
}

plot_pcoa()
The first two PCoA axes explain only about 10% of the variation together, so the plots capture only part of the community differences. Even so, they suggest effects of sampling date, latitude and habitat: northern samples gather in one direction, forest samples spread out along the first axis, and spring samples form a tail of their own. Homogenate and lysate samples overlap in most of the plot, but they are not fully mixed. The spring tail, for example, consists mainly of homogenate samples.

title: 6A. Within-sample diversity (track A: insects)
5B. Community differences (track B: marine plankton)
text:
Analyse differences in community composition between samples — beta diversity — using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).

Calculate Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
Bray-Curtis dissimilarity compares the abundances of taxa in two samples, from 0 for identical communities to 1 for communities with nothing in common. Both datasets use the same primers, so we can compare them at ASV level.
We give the columns the names that ecolongr expects by default, turn the counts into relative abundances so that sequencing depth does not affect the comparison, and calculate the dissimilarities:
asv_counts <- merged$counts |>
  transmute(sample = eventID, taxon = taxonID, quant = organismQuantity)

bray <- asv_counts |>
  el_decostand("total") |>
  el_vegdist("bray", samples = events$eventID)
el_decostand() and el_vegdist() work like decostand() and vegdist() in the vegan package, but on our table, without reading it into R. samples = makes the result follow the order of the rows in events, which we rely on when plotting. The result is an ordinary dist object that vegan and base R can use.


Run PCoA
Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) represents the dissimilarities among samples in a smaller number of dimensions:
pcoa <- cmdscale(bray, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

# Share of the positive eigenvalues held by each of the first two axes
axis_share <- pcoa$eig[1:2] / sum(pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0])
round(100 * axis_share, 1)


Plot PCoA results
We plot the PCoA once per dataset, with all samples in grey in the background. Colour shows the day of year and size the salinity, as on the maps:
plot_pcoa <- function() {
  xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(100 * axis_share[1]), "%)")
  ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(100 * axis_share[2]), "%)")
  x <- pcoa$points[, 1]
  y <- pcoa$points[, 2]

  layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE), heights = c(4, 1))
  par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

  for (dataset in c("2019-2020", "2013")) {
    ix <- events$dataset == dataset
    plot(x, y, col = "grey85", pch = 16, cex = 0.8,
         xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = dataset)
    points(x[ix], y[ix], pch = dataset_pch[dataset], col = "black",
           bg = color_yday[events$yday[ix]], cex = point_size(events$salinity[ix], 0.8, 15))
  }

  par(mar = c(3, 2, 1, 2))
  plot(1:366, rep(1, 366), col = color_yday, pch = "|", cex = 3,
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", ylim = c(0.9, 1.3))
  axis(1, at = c(1, 182, 366))
  text(183, 1.2, "Day of year")

  plot(c(2, 18, 34), rep(1, 3), pch = 1, cex = 0.8 + c(2, 18, 34) / 15,
       xlim = c(-5, 40), ylim = c(0.9, 1.3), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  axis(1, at = c(2, 18, 34))
  text(18, 1.2, "Salinity")
}

plot_pcoa()
The first axis explains about a third of the variation and follows salinity: the samples from the brackish Baltic Sea are on the left, and those from the saltier Kattegat and Skagerrak on the right. Within each group, the second axis follows the season. The samples from the 2013 transect fall in the same pattern as the later ones, which suggests that the two datasets can be compared.

title: Import and analyse ASV portal data with R
text:
This tutorial walks through the main steps for importing and analysing ASV portal data in R. The first two steps are the same for everyone. Then you choose one of two alternative tracks, which follow the same steps with different data:

Track A, insects: COI metabarcoding data from the Insect Biome Atlas (IBA) project, which sampled arthropods with Malaise traps at 200 sites across six habitat types in Sweden. We combine two datasets generated with different extraction protocols, homogenate and lysate.
Track B, marine plankton: 16S metabarcoding data of bacterioplankton from the Baltic Sea, from a transect sampled in 2013 and monitoring stations sampled in 2019–2020, along the salinity gradient from the Bothnian Bay to the Skagerrak.


Common steps

Environment setup — Access the workshop RStudio environment (or run locally), and choose your data
Data preparation — Load, merge and aggregate data from the ASV portal



Track A: Insects

Sample mapping — Filter, pair and map samples across Sweden and habitat types
Taxonomic composition — Barplots across habitats and months
Community differences (beta diversity) — Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and PCoA
Within-sample diversity (alpha diversity) — Shannon diversity across habitat types



Track B: Marine plankton

Sample mapping — Map samples and their salinity across the Baltic Sea
Taxonomic composition — Barplots across salinity and months
Community differences (beta diversity) — Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and PCoA
Within-sample diversity (alpha diversity) — Shannon diversity along the salinity gradient

Get started →

title: 4B. Taxonomic composition (track B: marine plankton)
text:
Summarise taxonomic composition across salinity and months using stacked barplots.

Sum reads by taxonomy
sum_clades_long() from step 2 can be limited to one taxonomic rank. The result is small enough to bring into R. We then add the salinity and month of each sample, and group the salinity into intervals:
salinity_breaks <- c(0, 3, 6, 12, 20, 35)

get_composition <- function(rank) {
  composition <- sum_clades_long(merged$counts, merged$asvs, ranks = rank) |>
    as.data.frame()
  composition <- merge(composition, events[c("eventID", "salinity", "month")], by = "eventID")
  composition$salinity_class <- cut(composition$salinity, salinity_breaks, right = FALSE)
  composition
}
Only the available ranks work here: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species and otu.


Define the barplot function
The function below identifies the most abundant taxa, calculates their mean relative abundance for each salinity interval and month, and draws stacked barplots with ggplot2. ggplot2 draws directly from a table with one row per value: each row of monthly becomes one segment of a bar.
plot_barplots <- function(rank, top_x = 10) {
  composition <- get_composition(rank)
  sampled <- events[!is.na(events$salinity), ]
  sampled$salinity_class <- cut(sampled$salinity, salinity_breaks, right = FALSE)

  # Absent taxa have no rows, so a mean is the sum divided by the number of samples
  totals <- tapply(composition$norm, composition$clade, sum)
  top <- names(sort(totals / nrow(sampled), decreasing = TRUE))[1:top_x]

  monthly <- aggregate(norm ~ clade + salinity_class + month,
                       composition[composition$clade %in% top, ], sum)
  n_samples <- aggregate(eventID ~ salinity_class + month, sampled, length)
  monthly <- merge(monthly, n_samples)
  monthly$share <- monthly$norm / monthly$eventID

  # Reversed levels put the most abundant taxon at the bottom of each bar
  monthly$clade <- factor(monthly$clade, levels = rev(top))
  monthly$month <- factor(monthly$month, levels = 1:12, labels = month.abb)

  mycols <- colorRampPalette(c(
    "#a6cee3", "#1f78b4", "#b2df8a", "#33a02c",
    "#fb9a99", "#e31a1c", "#fdbf6f", "#ff7f00",
    "#cab2d6", "#6a3d9a", "#ffff99", "#b15928"
  ))

  ggplot(monthly, aes(x = month, y = share, fill = clade)) +
    geom_col(colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.2) +
    facet_wrap(~salinity_class, ncol = 1, labeller = label_both) +
    scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(mycols(top_x), top), breaks = top, name = rank) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean share of reads") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}


Example: plot top classes
Plot the eight most abundant classes across salinity and months:
plot_barplots(rank = "class", top_x = 8)
Bacteroidia and Alphaproteobacteria are common at all salinities. Acidimicrobiia and Actinomycetes are more common in the least salty water, and Cyanobacteriia increase in summer. Many reads cannot be assigned to a class (Unclassified). Note that these are shares of the reads, not of the number of cells. Empty months had no samples in that salinity interval.

title: 3A. Sample mapping (track A: insects)
text:
Explore the spatial distribution of samples and their associated habitat types across Sweden.

Inspect contextual data
Core sample-level metadata is available in merged$events, an ordinary data frame with one row per sample:
events <- merged$events
colnames(events)



Extract temporal variables
Latitude and longitude can be used directly, whereas eventDate requires some preparation because dates in these two datasets are stored as start/end intervals. We therefore first extract the start of each interval before calculating month and day of year.
A few records only contain a year and no exact date. These cannot be assigned a month or day of year, so they are left as NA. We exclude these records below when filtering the samples used in the analyses.
event_start <- lubridate::parse_date_time(
  sub("/.*", "", events$eventDate),
  orders = c("ymd_HMSz", "ymd_HMS", "ymd"),
  quiet = TRUE
)
events$month <- lubridate::month(event_start)
events$yday  <- lubridate::yday(event_start)
events$date  <- as.Date(event_start)



Extract habitat type
The env_local_scale column contains habitat type classifications based on the Environment Ontology (ENVO). We first inspect the unique values:
unique(events$env_local_scale)
For plotting, we create short labels and assign a colour to each habitat:
habitat_map <- c(
  "forested area [ENVO:00000111]"    = "forest",
  "area of cropland [ENVO:01000892]" = "cropland",
  "wetland area [ENVO:00000043]"     = "wetland",
  "grassland area [ENVO:00000106]"   = "grassland",
  "urban biome [ENVO:01000249]"      = "urban",
  "alpine biome [ENVO:01001835]"     = "alpine"
)
events$habitat <- unname(habitat_map[events$env_local_scale])

habitat_cols <- c(
  "forest"    = "#2d6a4f",
  "cropland"  = "#d4a017",
  "wetland"   = "#4895ef",
  "grassland" = "#95d5b2",
  "urban"     = "#adb5bd",
  "alpine"    = "#9b5de5"
)



Filter samples
Samples with very few total reads are excluded, as their community composition is unreliable, and so are the handful with an incomplete eventDate. We get the sequencing depth of each sample with a query on the counts table:
depth <- merged$counts |>
  summarise(depth = sum(organismQuantity, na.rm = TRUE), .by = eventID) |>
  as.data.frame()

events <- merge(events, depth, by = "eventID")
summary(events$depth)  # inspect before picking a threshold

samples <- events[events$depth >= 100000 & !is.na(events$yday), ]
nrow(samples)
100000 is a reasonable depth threshold here. Check the summary() output above and adjust it if it excludes far more or fewer samples than expected for your dataset.



Pair the two extraction methods
The two datasets differ in size (homogenate: ~860 samples; lysate: ~4,550), and they do not cover the same places and dates. To compare the extraction methods fairly, we keep only samples from site and date combinations that occur in both, so that differences between the methods are not mixed up with differences between sites and seasons:
samples$method <- sub(":.*", "", samples$eventID)
samples$site_date <- paste(samples$locationID, samples$date)

shared <- Reduce(intersect, split(samples$site_date, samples$method))
samples <- samples[samples$site_date %in% shared, ]
table(samples$method)
From here on, samples is the fixed set of samples used throughout the rest of the tutorial. Each site and date occurs twice, once per extraction method. Remember this if you interpret habitat or season, since the two samples of a pair are not independent.



Map samples
We define a function that plots monthly maps of the study area, showing where and when samples were collected, with point colour indicating habitat type:
plot_monthly_maps <- function() {
  newmap <- rworldmap::getMap(resolution = "low")
  par(mfrow = c(4, 4), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1), xpd = TRUE)

  for (m in 1:12) {
    in_month <- samples[samples$month == m, ]
    plot(newmap, xlim = c(10, 25), ylim = c(55, 70), asp = 1, main = month.abb[m])
    if (nrow(in_month) > 0) {
      points(in_month$decimalLongitude, in_month$decimalLatitude, pch = 21,
             col = "black", bg = habitat_cols[in_month$habitat], cex = 1.5)
    }
  }

  plot.new()
  legend("left", bty = "n", legend = names(habitat_cols),
         pt.bg = habitat_cols, pch = 21, pt.cex = 1.6, cex = 1.1,
         title = "Habitat")
}

plot_monthly_maps()
This figure has several panels and can look cramped on a laptop screen. Click Zoom above the Plots pane for a larger view. Points also overlap since paired samples share a location, and nearby sites (~10–15 km apart) can coincide at this scale, so it looks sparser than the actual sample count.

title: 3B. Sample mapping (track B: marine plankton)
text:
Explore the spatial and seasonal distribution of the Baltic Sea samples, and their salinity.
The two datasets are 16S metabarcoding data of bacterioplankton from the Baltic Sea: a transect sampled in July 2013 (KTH-2013-Baltic-16S) and monitoring stations sampled in 2019–2020 (PRJEB55296-16S).

Inspect contextual data
Core sample-level metadata is available in merged$events, an ordinary data frame with one row per sample. We note which dataset each sample comes from:
events <- merged$events
dataset_labels <- c("KTH-2013-Baltic-16S" = "2013", "PRJEB55296-16S" = "2019-2020")
events$dataset <- unname(dataset_labels[events$datasetID])
table(events$dataset)



Check primers
Datasets can only be compared at ASV level if they were sequenced with the same primers:
unique(events[c("dataset", "pcr_primer_name_forward", "pcr_primer_name_reverse")])
Both datasets use the same primers.



Extract temporal variables
eventDate holds the date and time of sampling. We extract month and day of year:
event_start <- lubridate::parse_date_time(
  sub("/.*", "", events$eventDate),
  orders = c("ymd_HMSz", "ymd_HMS", "ymd_HM", "ymd"),
  quiet = TRUE
)
events$month <- lubridate::month(event_start)
events$yday  <- lubridate::yday(event_start)



Extract salinity
Salinity is one of the contextual measurements in emof, which has one row per measurement. The two datasets name it differently, so we first look at the names:
merged$emof |>
  filter(grepl("salinity", measurementType)) |>
  distinct(measurementType, measurementUnit) |>
  as.data.frame()
Some names end with a space, so we remove spaces at the ends before we pick out the salinity of each sample. This table is small, so we bring it into R first:
salinity <- merged$emof |>
  filter(grepl("salinity", measurementType)) |>
  as.data.frame()
salinity$measurementType <- trimws(salinity$measurementType)
salinity <- salinity[salinity$measurementType %in% c("salinity", "salinity_average"), ]

events$salinity <- as.numeric(salinity$measurementValue[match(events$eventID, salinity$eventID)])
summary(events$salinity)
Some samples have no salinity measurement. They are drawn with the smallest point size, and left out of the comparisons with salinity below.



Map samples
Point colour shows the day of year, point size the salinity, and the shape the dataset:
# Point size grows with salinity; samples without salinity get the smallest size
point_size <- function(salinity, base, step) base + ifelse(is.na(salinity), 0, salinity / step)

color_yday <- colorRampPalette(
  c("#2c7fb8", "#addd8e", "#edf8b1", "#fa9fb5", "#2c7fb8")
)(366)
dataset_pch <- c("2013" = 21, "2019-2020" = 22)

plot_maps <- function(dataset) {
  in_dataset <- events[events$dataset == dataset, ]
  newmap <- rworldmap::getMap(resolution = "low")
  par(mfrow = c(4, 4), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1), xpd = TRUE)

  for (m in 1:12) {
    in_month <- in_dataset[in_dataset$month %in% m, ]
    plot(newmap, xlim = c(10, 25), ylim = c(54, 66), asp = 1, main = month.abb[m])
    if (nrow(in_month) > 0) {
      points(in_month$decimalLongitude, in_month$decimalLatitude,
             pch = dataset_pch[dataset], col = "black",
             bg = color_yday[in_month$yday], cex = point_size(in_month$salinity, 1, 20))
    }
  }

  plot(1:366, rep(1, 366), col = color_yday, pch = "|", cex = 3,
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", ylim = c(0.9, 1.3))
  axis(1, at = c(1, 182, 366))
  text(183, 1.2, "Day of year", cex = 1.2)

  plot(c(2, 18, 34), rep(1, 3), pch = 1, cex = 1 + c(2, 18, 34) / 20,
       xlim = c(-5, 40), ylim = c(0.9, 1.3), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  axis(1, at = c(2, 18, 34))
  text(18, 1.2, "Salinity", cex = 1.2)
}

plot_maps("2019-2020")
The same function shows the 2013 transect:
plot_maps("2013")
These figures have several panels and can look cramped on a laptop screen. Click Zoom above the Plots pane for a larger view.

title: 2. Data preparation
text:
Load and combine ASV portal data, and summarise read counts by taxonomy.

How the data look
ASV read counts are often stored in wide format, with one row per ASV and one column per sample. The ASV portal instead uses long format, with one row per ASV–sample combination.



Wide



ASV
sample 1
sample 2




ASV a
620
251


ASV b
14

Long



eventID
taxonID
organismQuantity




sample 1
ASV a
620


sample 1
ASV b
14


sample 2
ASV a
251






Most ASVs occur in only a few samples. Long format lets us omit the many zeros, making it suitable for large datasets.



Load the datasets
We use two tools to work with large datasets without loading everything into R:

Parquet stores data efficiently in files on disk.
DuckDB analyses these files and returns only the results we request.

Load the data from the data_path folder defined in the previous section:
loaded <- load_long(data_path, store = store_path)
load_long() converts the data to Parquet files on the first run and reuses them later. These files are already prepared on the workshop machine. loaded contains one table per data type, covering all datasets.



Merge the datasets
Merge the datasets for joint analysis:
merged <- merge_long(loaded)
merge_long() checks for duplicate events (error) and conflicting ASV taxonomy between datasets (warning). The resulting merged list contains:

counts: ASV read counts
asvs: ASV sequences and taxonomy, one row per ASV
emof: contextual measurements (extended measurement or fact)
events: sample metadata (where, when, how, who)
datasets: dataset metadata
iasvs: ASVs with conflicting taxonomy, or NULL if none

Some tables may not appear in RStudio’s Environment pane. Use names() to see all elements:
names(loaded)
names(merged)
Instead of iasvs, loaded contains store, the path to the Parquet files.
For function documentation:
?asvoccur::load_long
?asvoccur::merge_long



Work with lazy tables
The large tables (counts, asvs and emof) are lazy: DuckDB reads data from the Parquet files only when needed. The smaller tables (events, datasets and iasvs) are ordinary R data frames.
Inspect the tables:
sapply(merged, \(x) class(x)[1])  # lazy tables are "prudent_duckplyr_df"
colnames(merged$asvs)
dim(merged$events)                # an ordinary data frame: samples and columns
We use familiar dplyr commands through the duckplyr package. For example, count the rows, samples and ASVs:
merged$counts |>
  summarise(rows = n(), samples = n_distinct(eventID), asvs = n_distinct(taxonID)) |>
  as.data.frame()
as.data.frame() executes the query and brings the result into R. Summarising or selecting rows first avoids loading the entire table.
Inspect a few rows:
merged$counts |> head(3) |> as.data.frame()
merged$asvs |> select(taxonID, phylum, order, genus, species) |> head(3) |> as.data.frame()
See which contextual measurements are available:
merged$emof |> distinct(measurementType, measurementUnit) |> as.data.frame()
ASVs with identical sequences are combined across datasets using SBDI ASV IDs (MD5 hashes of the sequences).
If a query cannot be translated to DuckDB, it gives an error rather than silently loading the entire table into R.



Aggregate counts by taxonomy
Sum ASV read counts at different taxonomic levels:
clades <- sum_clades_long(merged$counts, merged$asvs)
The result has one row per clade and sample, at levels from kingdom (or domain) to species, including otu if available:

raw: read counts
norm: proportion of reads in the sample (relative abundance)

The result is also lazy. To inspect phylum-level counts:
clades |>
  filter(rank == "phylum") |>
  head(3) |>
  as.data.frame()
ASVs missing an annotation at a given level are grouped as Unclassified. Existing annotation names such as unclassified.Acrididae are preserved.

title: 1. Environment setup
text: Set up the R environment used in the tutorial, either via the workshop cloud environment or locally on your laptop.

title: 1. Environment setup
text:
Option A (recommended): Workshop RStudio environment
A virtual machine running RStudio Server in PDC Cloud is available during the workshop. You will get a link, a username and a password.
Resources are shared, so avoid creating additional large objects. The machine shuts down after the workshop, so save your work as an R script and download it via the Files pane (More → Export) before you leave.

Check required packages
All required packages are pre-installed in the workshop environment. Load them and confirm that they are available:
library(asvoccur)
library(duckplyr)
library(ecolongr)
library(vegan)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)


Check access to example data
For this tutorial, ASV portal data is pre-downloaded and available on the virtual machine. It has also been prepared once for everyone, in shared folders called stores. Choose your track and set the paths:

Track A: InsectsTrack B: Marine plankton


data_path  <- "/srv/course-data/insects"
store_path <- "/srv/course-store/insects"
list.files(data_path)
If two (IBA_CO1) zip files are listed, you are ready to proceed.


data_path  <- "/srv/course-data/plankton"
store_path <- "/srv/course-store/plankton"
list.files(data_path)
If two (16S) zip files are listed, you are ready to proceed.

title: 1. Environment setup
section: Option B (fallback): Run RStudio locally on your laptop
text:
Option B (fallback): Run RStudio locally on your laptop
You will need to install:

R
RStudio
tools for compiling R packages, because ecolongr contains C++ code:

macOS: run xcode-select --install in the Terminal
Windows: Rtools, in the version that matches your R
Linux: usually the build-essential and r-base-dev packages

the following R packages:

remotes
asvoccur
duckplyr
ecolongr
vegan
rworldmap
lubridate
ggplot2


To install and load the required R packages:
# Install from CRAN
install.packages(c(
  "remotes",
  "duckplyr",
  "vegan",
  "rworldmap",
  "lubridate",
  "ggplot2"
))

# Install from GitHub
remotes::install_github("biodiversitydata-se/asvoccur@v1.3.0")
remotes::install_github("biodiversitydata-se/ecolongr@0.1.1")

# Load
library(asvoccur)
library(duckplyr)
library(ecolongr)
library(vegan)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

# Confirm versions
packageVersion("asvoccur")  # Should say 1.3.0
packageVersion("ecolongr")  # Should say 0.1.1

Download example data from the ASV portal
In this option, example data is downloaded directly from the ASV portal.

Go to the ASV portal start page.
Click DOWNLOAD. If you are not already logged in, you will be redirected to the login page.
If you do not already have an account, either:

sign in with a Google or GitHub account, or
create a new SBDI account.

On the Download page, under Download link, download the two datasets of the track you have chosen:

Track A, insects: IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE and IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE
Track B, marine plankton: KTH-2013-Baltic-16S and PRJEB55296-16S

Place the two zip files in a folder of their own, e.g.:
course-data/
└── insects/
    ├── IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE.zip
    └── IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE.zip
Set the paths in R and confirm access. The store is a new folder that is created in the next step:

data_path  <- "local/path/to/course-data/insects"
store_path <- "local/path/to/course-store/insects"
list.files(data_path)
If the expected zip file(s) are listed, you are ready to proceed.
